Count Rouvaloff stared at him in astonishment for a few moments. Then, realizing that he was entirely serious, he wrote an address on a piece of paper, added his initials, and passed it across the table.

“Scotland Yard would pay a great deal to learn this address, my dear fellow.”

“They won’t get it,” Lord Arthur exclaimed with a laugh. He shook the young Russian’s hand warmly, ran downstairs, read the paper, and instructed his coachman to drive to Soho Square.

There he sent the coachman away and walked down Greek Street until he reached a place called Bayle’s Court. Passing through the archway, he entered a curious little dead end apparently occupied by a French laundry: clotheslines formed a complete network between the houses, and white linen fluttered in the morning breeze. He went all the way to the end and knocked at a small green house. After a delay, during which every window around the court filled with a blur of watching faces, a rather rough-looking foreigner opened the door and asked his business in very poor English. Lord Arthur gave him Count Rouvaloff’s note. On seeing it, the man bowed and showed him into a very shabby front sitting room on the ground floor. Moments later, Herr Winckelkopf, as he was known in England, bustled in, wearing a heavily wine-stained napkin around his neck and holding a fork in his left hand.

“Count Rouvaloff has given me an introduction to you,” Lord Arthur said with a bow, “and I’d like to speak briefly with you about a business matter. My name is Smith, Mr. Robert Smith, and I want you to supply an explosive clock.”

“Delighted to meet you, Lord Arthur,” said the friendly little German, laughing. “Don’t look so alarmed. Knowing everyone is part of my duty, and I remember seeing you one evening at Lady Windermere’s. I hope her ladyship is well. Would you sit with me while I finish breakfast? The pâté is excellent, and my friends are kind enough to say that my Rhine wine surpasses anything served at the German Embassy.” Before Lord Arthur had recovered from the surprise of being recognized, he was sitting in the back room, drinking exquisite Marcobrünner from a pale yellow Rhine-wine glass bearing the Imperial monogram and chatting on the friendliest possible terms with the celebrated conspirator.

“Explosive clocks,” Herr Winckelkopf observed, “aren’t especially suitable for export abroad. Even when they get through customs, the trains run so irregularly that the clocks usually explode before arriving at the intended destination.

Emma did not regret lowering herself enough to visit the Coles. The following day, she had many pleasant memories of the evening. Whatever dignity she might have lost by giving up her usual distance from such company was surely repaid by the glory of being so popular. She must have delighted the Coles—good people who deserved to be happy! And she must have left them with an impression they would not soon forget.

Perfect happiness is rare, even when we look back on an event, and two things troubled her. She wondered whether she had failed in the loyalty one woman owed another by telling Frank Churchill what she suspected about Jane Fairfax’s feelings. It had hardly been right. But the idea had taken such a strong hold of her that it had slipped out. And his acceptance of everything she said had so flattered her powers of observation that she found it difficult to feel certain she should have kept quiet.

Her other regret also concerned Jane Fairfax, and about this one she had no doubts. She sincerely and completely regretted that her own playing and singing were so much poorer. She deeply mourned the time she had wasted as a child, then sat down and practised hard for an hour and a half.

Harriet’s arrival interrupted her. If Harriet’s praise could have satisfied her, she would soon have felt better.

“Oh, if only I could play as well as you and Miss Fairfax!”

“Don’t put us together, Harriet. My playing is no more like hers than lamplight is like sunshine.”

“Oh, dear—I think you’re the better player. I think you play every bit as well as she does. I’m sure I would much rather listen to you. Everyone last night said how well you played.”

“Anyone who understood music must have heard the difference. The truth, Harriet, is that I play just well enough to earn praise, but Jane Fairfax is far beyond that.”

“Well, I’ll always think you play just as well as she does, or that any difference is too small for anyone to notice. Mr. Cole spoke about your wonderful taste, and Mr. Frank Churchill talked a great deal about it too. He said he valued musical taste much more than technical skill.”

“Ah, but Jane Fairfax has both, Harriet.”

“Are you sure? I could see that she had technical skill, but I didn’t know she had any taste. Nobody mentioned it. And I hate singing in Italian—you can’t understand a word. Besides, even if she does play so wonderfully, it’s only what she has to do, because she’ll have to teach.

A little after noon, the boys borrowed a small rowing boat from a townsman who was away and set off immediately. When they were several miles downstream from Cave Hollow, Tom said:

“Now, see how this cliff looks the same all the way down from the cave hollow? No houses, no places storing wood, and the same bushes everywhere. But can you see that white patch up there where the ground slid down? Well, that’s one of my landmarks. We’ll go ashore here.”

They landed.

“Now, Huck, from where we’re standing, you could reach the hole I escaped through with a fishing pole. See if you can find it.”

Huck searched all around without finding anything. Tom proudly walked into a thick patch of sumac bushes and said:

“Here it is! Look, Huck. It’s the best hidden hole anywhere around. Just keep quiet about it. I’ve wanted to be a robber all along, but I knew I needed a place like this. Finding one was the problem. Now we’ve got it, and we’ll keep it secret, except we’ll tell Joe Harper and Ben Rogers. Of course we need a gang, or it wouldn’t have any style. Tom Sawyer’s Gang—sounds splendid, doesn’t it, Huck?”

“It certainly does, Tom. Who are we going to rob?”

“Oh, just about anybody. You wait beside the road and surprise people—that’s the usual way.”

“And kill them?”

“No, not always. You keep them in the cave until they get a ransom together.”

“What’s a ransom?”

“Money. You make them get all they can from their friends. After you’ve kept them for a year, if they still haven’t got it, you kill them. That’s the usual way. Except you don’t kill women. You lock them up, but you never kill them. They’re always beautiful and rich and terribly frightened. You take their watches and things, but you always remove your hat and speak politely. Nobody’s as polite as robbers—you’ll see that in any book. Then the women start loving you. After a week or two in the cave, they stop crying, and after that you couldn’t make them leave. If you chased them out, they’d turn straight around and come back. That’s what happens in all the books.”

“Why, that sounds wonderful, Tom. I think it’s better than being a pirate.”

“Yes, it’s better in some ways, because you’re close to home and circuses and everything.”

By now everything was ready, and the boys entered the hole with Tom leading. They struggled through to the tunnel’s far end, secured the kite strings they had tied together, and went on.
